title: Multi-Cluster Multi-Level Visualization with plot_mcml: A Complete Guide
text: Large networks many nodes multiple constructs, components, factors fundamental problem hard work . Consider network 20 nodes, representing construct: motivation, engagement, emotions, collaboration. network 400 possible connections, making difficult interpret directly. common solution concatenate nodes lose internal relations, plot 400 edges get lost details. Multi-Cluster Multi-Level network (MCML, despite long name) designed solve problem. works creating network within cluster showing connections summarizing inter-cluster connections macro-level network. way, preserve data integrity value fine-grained details. Think MCML network networks. MCML workflow critical analytical advantage: built, macro network cluster network full TNA networks right. means can compute centrality, run bootstrap stability analysis, permutation tests, even higher-order pathway analysis (HYPA) cluster independently. MCML just visualization — decomposition complex network interpretable, analyzable sub-networks. Installation cograph Nestimate CRAN. Nestimate handles MCML computation (build_mcml, as_tna); cograph handles visualization (plot_mcml, splot).
code: #install.packages("cograph") #install.packages("Nestimate")

title: Multi-Cluster Multi-Level Visualization with plot_mcml: A Complete Guide
text: use human_long dataset bundled Nestimate — 10,796 coded human actions 429 human-AI programming sessions. coding scheme 9 codes grouped 3 clusters — codes become nodes, clusters become groups. plot_mcml() models levels simultaneously single figure. bottom layer shows every node inside cluster full edges drawn cluster level. top layer collapses cluster single macro-level node, edges carrying aggregated inter-cluster flow. Dashed inter-layer lines connect node cluster’s macro node, making hierarchical mapping explicit. Directive — human telling AI (commanding, specifying requirements, requesting) Evaluative — human judging AI output (correcting, expressing frustration, refining, verifying) Metacognitive — human stepping back think redirect (inquiring, interrupting) Figure 1: MCML: cluster networks , macro network Clusters can defined three ways. produce result: Named list (common): Data frame node group columns: Extracted data grouping variable already exists: Clusters Come ? Theory: Define groups based domain knowledge, . Community detection: Use detect_communities() cograph discover structure algorithmically. External grouping variables: nodes metadata (e.g., department, brain region, country), use . as_tna() converts MCML individual networks — macro network one network per cluster: element full TNA network can plotted, analyzed, bootstrapped independently: Figure 2: MCML decomposed individual networks: macro + cluster
code: data("human_long", package = "Nestimate")  net <- build_network(   human_long,   actor = "session_id", action = "code", time = "timestamp",   method = "relative" )  clusters <- list(   Directive     = c("Specify", "Command", "Request"),   Evaluative    = c("Verify", "Frustrate", "Correct", "Refine"),   Metacognitive = c("Interrupt", "Inquire") )  mcml_obj <- Nestimate::build_mcml(net, clusters, type = "tna") mcml_obj MCML Network ============ Type: tna  | Method: sum Nodes: 9  | Clusters: 3 Transitions: 10270   Macro: 5188  | Per-cluster: 5082  Clusters:   Directive (3): Specify, Command, Request   Evaluative (4): Verify, Frustrate, Correct, Refine   Metacognitive (2): Interrupt, Inquire  Macro (cluster-level) weights:               Directive Evaluative Metacognitive Directive        0.6056     0.2241        0.1703 Evaluative       0.4774     0.4057        0.1169 Metacognitive    0.4170     0.3275        0.2555 splot(mcml_obj) clusters <- list(   Directive     = c("Specify", "Command", "Request"),   Evaluative    = c("Verify", "Frustrate", "Correct", "Refine"),   Metacognitive = c("Interrupt", "Inquire") ) clusters_df <- data.frame(   node  = c("Specify", "Command", "Request",             "Verify", "Frustrate", "Correct", "Refine",             "Interrupt", "Inquire"),   group = c(rep("Directive", 3), rep("Evaluative", 4), rep("Metacognitive", 2)) ) clusters_auto <- split(human_long$code, human_long$cluster) |> lapply(unique) grp <- Nestimate::as_tna(mcml_obj) names(grp) [1] "macro"         "Directive"     "Evaluative"    "Metacognitive" splot(grp)

title: Multi-Cluster Multi-Level Visualization with plot_mcml: A Complete Guide
text: cluster assigned one color propagates consistently across every visual element: shell fill, node fill, within-cluster edges, pie-chart slice top layer, legend entry. colors NULL (default), colorblind-safe palette generated automatically. override , pass character vector one color per cluster, order cluster list. Choose colors sufficient contrast clusters — avoid hues similar. Muted, low-saturation palettes work well publication figures, saturated palettes effective slides posters: Figure 10: Custom cluster colors layers support four shapes: "circle" (default), "square", "diamond", "triangle". node_shape parameter controls detail nodes bottom layer, cluster_shape controls summary pie-chart nodes top layer. can single value (applied uniformly) vector length number nodes clusters, allowing per-element customization. Mixing shapes layers helps reader distinguish two levels glance. example , detail nodes use diamonds cluster’s summary node gets different shape: Figure 11: Diamond nodes mixed macro shapes Three size parameters control main visual elements independently. shape_size sets radius cluster’s elliptical shell bottom layer — increase nodes feel cramped inside shell. node_size controls individual detail nodes. summary_size controls pie-chart summary nodes top layer. Balancing three sizes determines visual hierarchy: large summary_size relative node_size draws reader’s eye macro level first, equalizing gives levels comparable visual weight: Figure 12: Larger shells nodes Cluster shells semi-transparent ellipses bottom layer visually group nodes. Two parameters control appearance: shell_alpha (fill transparency, 0–1) shell_border_width (border line width). Higher shell_alpha values create stronger visual grouping may obscure edges underneath; lower values keep shells subtle, letting network structure dominate. Increasing shell_border_width makes cluster boundaries prominent, helps shells overlap slightly: Figure 13: Thick borders, opaque shells Fine-tune borders layers independently. Detail nodes accept node_border_color; summary pie-chart nodes accept summary_border_color summary_border_width: Figure 14: Left: dark heavy borders; Right: colored borders matching clusters colored slice summary pie chart can represent two different quantities, controlled summary_pie: "inits" (default) — cluster’s share initial state distribution. Answers: “often sequences start cluster?” "self" — cluster’s self-retention ratio (self-loop weight / total -strength). Answers: “sticky cluster — much flow stays inside?” Figure 15: Left: initial state distribution; Right: self-retention ratio mostly-colored pie "inits" means cluster common starting point. "self", means cluster retains outgoing flow internally — transitions loop back rather escaping clusters. building macro network individual edges, aggregation parameter controls pairwise weights collapse cluster--cluster values: "sum" (default) — total flow volume. Larger clusters naturally produce higher values. "mean" — average flow per node pair. Normalizes cluster size differences. "max" — strongest single edge. Highlights dominant connection. Figure 16: Sum emphasizes volume; mean normalizes size; max finds dominant link

title: Network Estimation and Visualization with Nestimate + cograph
text: Nestimate unified network estimation package R. provides single entry point — build_network() — accepts sequence data, wide-format behavioral data, numeric matrices estimates networks using 10 built-methods. result netobject inherits cograph_network, every object produced Nestimate can plotted splot() directly. core design principle estimation visualization separate concerns: Nestimate handles computation (network construction, bootstrapping, permutation testing, clustering, multi-cluster analysis), cograph handles rendering. separation means analyst writes estimation code gets publication-ready figures without adapter code manual class conversion. Beyond single-network estimation, Nestimate provides complete statistical toolkit: Bootstrap stability analysis (bootstrap_network) — identifies edges survive resampling sampling artifacts. Permutation-based group comparison (permutation) — tests whether edges differ significantly conditions. Multi-cluster multi-level analysis (csum, summarize_clusters) — aggregates node-level networks cluster-level summaries hierarchical visualization. Centrality stability (centrality_stability) — assesses whether centrality rankings robust case dropping. Group-level operations — bootstrapping, permutation testing, plotting work grouped networks additional code. tutorial walks full pipeline group_regulation_long dataset shipped Nestimate.

Undirected methods (glasso, pcor, cor, co_occurrence, ising) model co-occurrence partial correlation structures — behaviors tend appear together. choice method driven theoretical question, convenience. netobject works splot(): Figure 2: Frequency-based transition network (raw counts) Figure 3: Co-occurrence network (undirected)
code: list_estimators() name                                                description 1          attention                       Decay-weighted attention transitions 2      co_occurrence                             Co-occurrence within sequences 3                cor                               Pairwise correlation network 4          frequency                            Raw transition frequency counts 5             glasso                EBICglasso regularized partial correlations 6              ising             Ising model (L1-penalized logistic regression) 7                mgm Mixed Graphical Model (nodewise lasso, EBIC, LW threshold) 8               pcor                         Unregularized partial correlations 9           relative                    Row-normalized transition probabilities 10              wtna                     Window-based TNA transitions (one-hot) 11 wtna_cooccurrence                   Window-based TNA co-occurrence (one-hot)    directed 1      TRUE 2     FALSE 3     FALSE 4      TRUE 5     FALSE 6     FALSE 7     FALSE 8     FALSE 9      TRUE 10     TRUE 11    FALSE frequency_net    <- build_network(group_regulation_long, action = "Action",                                   actor = "Actor", method = "frequency") attention_net    <- build_network(group_regulation_long, action = "Action",                                   actor = "Actor", method = "attention") co_occurrence_net <- build_network(group_regulation_long, action = "Action",                                    actor = "Actor", method = "co_occurrence") splot(frequency_net) splot(co_occurrence_net, layout = "spring")

title: Network Estimation and Visualization with Nestimate + cograph
text: common analytical question : given network individual states (nodes), can group meaningful clusters study clusters interact? MCML (Multi-Cluster Multi-Level) pipeline exactly . aggregates node-level network cluster-level summary, producing macro-level view (cluster--cluster transitions) per-cluster detail networks (within-cluster structure). several ways build MCML analysis, depending whether start pre-built network raw data, whether define clusters manually discover algorithmically. domain knowledge dictates grouping, define clusters named list node labels pass csum(). collaborative regulation, can distinguish regulatory behaviors (monitoring, planning, coregulating, adapting) social-communicative behaviors (cohesion, consensus, discussion, emotion, synthesis): splot() dispatches mcml object plot_mcml(), rendering two-layer visualization: bottom layer shows within-cluster detail networks, top layer shows macro (cluster--cluster) summary. Figure 17: MCML — theory-driven two-cluster partition (Regulatory vs. Social) summarize_clusters() provides result slightly different interface. given netobject, uses pre-computed weight matrix:  strong theoretical grouping exists, Nestimate::cluster_network() discovers clusters algorithmically. clusters raw sequence data (using PAM default) builds separate network per cluster, returning netobject_group: as_tna() converts MCML result netobject_group — named list containing macro network per-cluster network individual netobject objects. useful want analyze cluster’s network independently (e.g., compute centrality, run bootstrap) pass functions. Figure 18: MCML converted individual networks — macro + per-cluster panels summarize_network() cograph takes different approach: instead two-layer MCML visualization, collapses node-level network single cluster-level cograph_network cluster becomes one node. useful need macro view. Figure 19: Cluster-level summary network — one node per cluster, aggregated edge weights MCML approaches summary
code: clusters <- list(   Regulatory = c("monitor", "plan", "coregulate", "adapt"),   Social     = c("cohesion", "consensus", "discuss", "emotion", "synthesis") )  mcml_theory <- csum(net, clusters, type = "tna") mcml_theory Cluster Summary --------------- Type: tna Method: sum Clusters: 2 Nodes: 9 Cluster sizes: 4, 5  Macro (cluster-level) weights (2x2):   Inits: 0.318, 0.682            Regulatory Social Regulatory      0.302  0.698 Social          0.332  0.668  Per-cluster weights:   Regulatory (4 nodes)   Social (5 nodes) splot(mcml_theory) mcml_built <- summarize_clusters(net, clusters, type = "tna") splot(mcml_built) #grp_clustered <- Nestimate::cluster_network(group_regulation_long, k = 3) #names(grp_clustered) #splot(grp_clustered) tna_models <- as_tna(mcml_theory) names(tna_models) [1] "macro"      "Regulatory" "Social" splot(tna_models) summary_net <- summarize_network(net, clusters) summary_net Cograph network: 2 nodes, 4 edges ( directed ) Source: matrix   Nodes (2): Regulatory, Social   Edges: 2 / 2 (density: 100.0%)   Weights: [1.660, 2.794]  |  mean: 2.227   Strongest edges:     Regulatory -> Social  2.794     Social -> Regulatory  1.660   Self-loops: 2  |  range: [1.206, 3.340] Layout: none   Use as.data.frame() for the edge table, as.data.frame(what = "nodes") for the nodes. splot(summary_net, node_size = 15, edge_labels = TRUE)

title: Network Visualization with cograph: A Complete Plotting Guide
text: Network visualization R traditionally meant choosing two extremes: quick--dirty plots look like hairballs, heavily customized code takes longer write analysis . cograph collapses tradeoff. splot() function produces publication-ready network visualizations single call, sensible defaults can override parameter parameter. tutorial demonstrates everything single TNA model collaborative regulation behaviors. start zero-argument plot progressively layer customization — can see exactly parameter changes. plot — one line, zero arguments, publication-ready Node styling — shapes, colors, sizes, labels, centrality-based scaling Edge styling — width, color, curvature, labels, thresholds Donuts pies — composite node shapes multivariate data Themes palettes — pre-built visual themes Pipe-friendly API — sn_* function family chainable plot building Specialized plots — chord diagrams, heatmaps, alluvial flows Group comparisons — difference networks multi-group grids Bootstrap — validated network visualization Permutation testing — significant group differences Mixed networks — directed undirected edges combined TNA-specific workflows, see TNA tutorial. GitHub Development Version tutorial covers full feature set available GitHub development version cograph. CRAN release provides core plotting engine; development version adds themes, pipe API, specialized plots, additional features.

title: Network Visualization with cograph: A Complete Plotting Guide
text: Overlay directed undirected edges plot. useful two types relationships — example, symmetric co-occurrence patterns asymmetric transition probabilities. defaults follow TNA conventions: oval layout, weight-scaled edges, dotted edge starts, visible edge labels. Figure 23: Co-occurrence (steel blue, straight) transitions (dark blue, curved) TNA-style defaults can distinguish edge types color: undirected co-occurrence edges straight steel-blue lines, directed transitions curved dark-blue arrows dotted starts. Edge widths scale automatically weight, stronger connections stand . Figure 24: Custom colors visually separate edge types
code: # Undirected: symmetric co-occurrence (half the weight for visual balance) set.seed(42) sym <- (model$weights + t(model$weights)) / 2 noise <- matrix(runif(length(sym), -0.02, 0.02), nrow = nrow(sym)) noise <- (noise + t(noise)) / 2  # keep symmetric diag(noise) <- 0 sym <- pmax(sym * 0.5 + noise, 0)  # Directed: original transition probabilities asym <- model$weights  # Defaults: oval layout, blue edges, weight-scaled widths, edge labels plot_mixed_network(sym, asym, threshold = 0.03,   title = "Co-occurrence + Transitions" ) plot_mixed_network(sym, asym, threshold = 0.03,   sym_color = "#E63946",   asym_color = "#003355",   title = "Red undirected + Blue directed" )

title: Advanced examples
text: Sophisticated edge labels showing confidence intervals significance.
code: # 9 named nodes nodes9 <- c("Explore", "Plan", "Execute", "Monitor",             "Adapt", "Reflect", "Regulate", "Review", "Learn")  # Denser weight matrix set.seed(99) mat9 <- matrix(runif(81, 0, 0.5), 9, 9, dimnames = list(nodes9, nodes9)) diag(mat9) <- 0 # Keep ~60% of edges mat9[mat9 < 0.2] <- 0  # Generate CI bounds and p-values set.seed(42) ci_lower <- mat9 * runif(81, 0.6, 0.8) ci_upper <- mat9 * runif(81, 1.2, 1.4) pvals <- matrix(NA, 9, 9) pvals[mat9 > 0] <- runif(sum(mat9 > 0), 0.0001, 0.08)  splot(mat9,   layout = "circle",   node_size = 8,   node_fill = "#4A90A4",   node_border_color = "#2C5F6E",   node_border_width = 2,   label_size = 0.6,   edge_color = "#666666",   edge_width = 1.5,   curvature = 0.15,   edge_ci_lower = ci_lower,   edge_ci_upper = ci_upper,   edge_label_p = pvals,   edge_label_stars = TRUE,   edge_label_style = "full",   edge_label_size = 0.65,   edge_label_color = "#800020" )

title: Migrating from qgraph to splot
text: splot() primary plotting engine cograph. renders network graphs using base R graphics designed work across wide range use cases: transition networks learning analytics, correlation networks psychology, social networks, weighted unweighted graph structure. accepts adjacency matrices, edge lists, igraph objects, tna objects, qgraph objects directly, fits existing workflows without requiring format conversion. function built useful every stage analysis. single call like splot(mat) produces clean, readable plot sensible defaults. need , function supports confidence interval underlays edges, significance stars derived p-values, templated edge labels combine estimates CI ranges stars (e.g., 0.25*** [0.12, 0.38]), pie donut charts nodes, publication-quality export 600 DPI. goal need switch tools analysis moves exploration final manuscript figure.

title: Migrating from qgraph to splot
text: One deliberate choices splot() consistent, predictable parameter naming system. Every parameter prefixed element controls – node_, edge_, label_, donut_, pie_, edge_label_, edge_ci_ – followed property: size, color, fill, width, alpha, . node_fill node fill color, edge_label_size edge label font size, donut_border_color donut border color, edge_ci_alpha confidence interval underlay transparency. naming designed learn pattern, can guess parameter names without checking documentation. contrasts conventions like vsize, posCol, border.width, label.cex, pieColor, every parameter follows different convention needs memorized individually.

title: Migrating from qgraph to splot
text: Network plots research often need communicate uncertainty significance alongside graph structure . splot() treats first-class concern rather afterthought. Edges can carry confidence interval underlays (edge_ci) – semi-transparent bands behind edge whose width reflects uncertainty estimate. Edge labels can built templates (edge_label_template) using placeholders like {est}, stars, {low}, {}, {range}, {p}, filled vectors CI bounds p-values supply. Significance stars computed automatically p-values edge_label_stars = TRUE. features mean single splot() call can produce network every edge shows weight, significance level, confidence interval – information otherwise require post-processing manual annotation.

Set TRUE force directed, FALSE force undirected. type Character string specifying degree correlation compute, NULL (default) choose automatically: "-" directed networks "degree" undirected ones. directed network accepted values "-", "-", "-" "-"; undirected network accepted value "degree". value raises error. digits Integer NULL. title: Degree Assortativity Coefficient — assortativity
text: degree assortativity coefficient defined Pearson correlation coefficient degrees nodes either end edge (Newman 2002): $$r = \frac{\sum_{jk} jk(e_{jk} - q_j q_k)}{\sigma_q^2}$$ \(e_{jk}\) fraction edges connecting degree-\(j\) degree-\(k\) vertices, \(q_k\) excess degree distribution, \(\sigma_q^2\) variance. Pearson correlation invariant subtracting constant, implementation computes correlation raw degrees two ends edge, counting every undirected edge orientations. numerically identical formula . Degrees unweighted counts edges, edge weights enter coefficient. directed networks, coefficient Pearson correlation source-end target-end degrees edge stored orientation, degree mode end chosen type (Foster et al. 2010). coefficient NA network edges either degree vector zero variance.

title: Access and Hide Information — centrality_access_information
text: Access hide information (Rosvall et al. 2005; Sneppen, Trusina Rosvall 2005) measure number bits walker needs follow shortest path without map. search information \(\) \(j\) sums shortest paths \(p(, j)\), \(k_i\) degree source \(k_l - 1\) choices left intermediate node: $$S(\j) = -\log_2 \sum_{p(, j)} \frac{1}{k_i}   \prod_{l \p,\, l \ne , j} \frac{1}{k_l - 1}.$$ Access information \(A_i\) averages \(S(\j)\) targets \(j\), hide information \(H_i\) averages \(S(j \)\) sources.

title: Community-Based Centralities — centrality_community_based

Comm centrality (Gupta, Singh Cherifi 2016) combines intra-community degree \(k^{}\) inter-community degree \(k^{}\): $$CC() = (1 + \mu_C) \frac{k^{}_i}{\max_{j \C} k^{}_j} R   + (1 - \mu_C)   \left(\frac{k^{}_i}{\max_{j \C} k^{}_j} R\right)^2,$$ \(\mu_C\) mean inter-link fraction community \(\). Community-based mediator centrality (Tulu, Hou Younas 2018) \(CbM() = H_i\, d_i / \sum_j d_j\), \(H_i\) base-2 entropy links \(\) communities.

title: WVoteRank, EnRenew and VoteRank++ — centrality_wvoterank
text: Three spreader-selection procedures VoteRank family elect one node per round. WVoteRank (Sun et al. 2019) scores node \(s_v = \sqrt{k_v \sum_{u \N(v)} va_u w_{vu}}\) lowers ability neighbors winner \(1 / \langle w \rangle\), inverse average strength. EnRenew (Guo et al. 2020) elects largest neighbor entropy \(E_v = -\sum_{u \N(v)} p_{uv} \ln p_{uv}\), \(p_{uv} = k_u / \sum_{l \N(v)} k_l\), scales entropy terms within enrenew_depth steps \(1 - 1 / (2^{d-1} \ln \langle k \rangle)\). VoteRank++ (Liu et al. 2021) starts ability \(\ln(1 + k_i / k_{\max})\), splits votes proportion degree, multiplies abilities \(\lambda\) one step winner \(\sqrt{\lambda}\) two steps away.

title: Project Bipartite Network to One-Mode — project_bipartite
text: Projects two-mode (bipartite/incidence) network one-mode adjacency matrix. Row-mode projection yields matrix shared-column connections among row nodes; column-mode projection converse.

title: Project Bipartite Network to One-Mode — project_bipartite

title: Project Bipartite Network to One-Mode — project_bipartite
text: x incidence matrix (rows = type 1 nodes, columns = type 2 nodes) non-zero entries indicate connections. Can also data.frame columns type1, type2, optionally weight. mode Character. "rows" (default) projects onto row nodes (result: n_rows x n_rows). "columns" projects onto column nodes (result: n_cols x n_cols). method Character. Projection method: "sum" Weighted projection: %*% t() (rows) t() %*% (columns). Edge weight equals sum shared connection-weight products. "binary" Co-occurrence count: binarize first, compute overlap. Edge weight equals number shared connections. "jaccard" Jaccard similarity: shared / (total_i + total_j - shared) pair. "cosine" Cosine similarity: dot product row (column) vectors divided product norms. "newman" Newman's weighted projection (Newman 2001): shared affiliation contributes 1 / (d_k - 1) d_k degree shared node. Gives weight connections exclusive affiliations. ... Additional arguments (currently unused).

title: Project Bipartite Network to One-Mode — project_bipartite
text: square adjacency matrix, one row column per node projected mode: n_rows x n_rows named rownames(x) mode = "rows", n_cols x n_cols named colnames(x) mode = "columns". diagonal set 0 (self-loops).

title: Project Bipartite Network to One-Mode — project_bipartite
text: method = "sum" method = "cosine" use incidence values . "binary", "jaccard" "newman" first binarize incidence matrix (x > 0), weights discarded three. Newman projection, affiliations shared one node focal type (d_k = 1) skipped, since 1 / (d_k - 1) undefined. follows convention Newman (2001).

title: Project Bipartite Network to One-Mode — project_bipartite

text: Edge curving controlled two interacting arguments: curves Mode automatic curving. title: Base R Graphics Network Plotting — splot.net_bootstrap
text: Controls edge weights mapped visual widths: "linear" (default) Width proportional weight. Best weights similar magnitude. "log" Logarithmic scaling. what: Donut vs Pie vs Double Donut
title: Base R Graphics Network Plotting — splot.net_bootstrap
text: Three ways show additional data nodes: Donut (donut_fill) Single ring showing proportion (0-1). Ideal completion rates, probabilities, single metric per node. Use donut_color fill color donut_bg_color unfilled portion. Pie (pie_values) Multiple colored segments showing category breakdown. Ideal composition data. Values normalized sum 1. Use pie_colors segment colors. Double donut (donut2_values) Two concentric rings comparing two metrics per node. Outer ring uses donut_fill/donut_color, inner ring uses donut2_values/donut2_colors.

what: Build MCML from Raw Transition Data — summarize_clusters
title: Build MCML from Raw Transition Data — summarize_clusters
text: Builds Multi-Cluster Multi-Level (MCML) model raw transition data (edge lists sequences) recoding node labels cluster labels counting observed transitions. macro network Markov chain cluster states. Weight matrices passed csum, aggregates .

title: Build MCML from Raw Transition Data — summarize_clusters
code: summarize_clusters(   x,   clusters = NULL,   method = c("sum", "mean", "median", "max", "min", "density", "geomean"),   type = c("tna", "frequency", "cooccurrence", "semi_markov", "raw"),   directed = TRUE,   compute_within = TRUE )

title: Build MCML from Raw Transition Data — summarize_clusters
text: x Input data. Accepts multiple formats: data.frame /columns Edge list. Columns named /source/src/v1/node1//target/tgt/v2/node2/j auto-detected. Optional weight column (weight/w/value/strength). data.frame without /columns Sequence data. row sequence, columns time steps. Consecutive pairs (t, t+1) become transitions. data frame three columns default names V1, V2, V3, ... read sequence data, even though V1 V2 also /names. tna object x$data non-NULL, uses sequence path raw data. Otherwise falls back csum. cograph_network x$data non-NULL, detects edge list vs sequence data. Otherwise falls back csum. group_tna Converted as_mcml. mcml cluster_summary Returned unchanged. square numeric matrix Falls back csum. non-square character matrix Treated sequence data. clusters Cluster/group assignments. Accepts: named list Direct mapping. List names = cluster names, values = character vectors node labels. Example: list(= c("N1","N2"), B = c("N3","N4")) data.frame data frame first column contains node names second column contains group/cluster names. Example: data.frame(node = c("N1","N2","N3"), group = c("","","B")) membership vector Character numeric vector. Node names extracted data. Example: c("","","B","B") column name string edge list data.frames, name column containing cluster labels. mapping built unique (node, group) pairs columns. NULL Auto-detect cograph_network$nodes $node_groups (logic csum). method Aggregation method combining edge weights: "sum", "mean", "median", "max", "min", "density", "geomean". Default "sum". type Post-processing: "tna" (row-normalize), "frequency" "raw" (normalization), "cooccurrence" (symmetrize), "semi_markov" (row-normalize, identical "tna"). Default "tna". directed Logical. Default TRUE. FALSE node-level weights symmetrized \((+ ^T) / 2\) aggregation: matrix input averaged transpose, observed transition counts half direction. value recorded meta$directed. compute_within Logical. Compute within-cluster matrices? Default TRUE.

title: Trophic Incoherence Parameter — trophic_incoherence

Normalised Shannon entropy node’s hop-distance profile; closeness mean profile, spread. normaliser log(M - m + 1) uniform profile scores exactly 1 (printed formula’s log(M - m) undefined two distances). centrality_local_dimension() (tau 0.50) — Pu et al. (2014). OLS slope ln B(r) ln r, ball including centre. Reproduces worked example Wen & Deng (2019) exactly (0.9231). Lower = influential. centrality_local_information_dimension() (tau 0.38) — Wen & Deng (2020). Entropy-weighted local dimension boxes half eccentricity. Higher = influential. Q(G, C) - Q(G - , C \ ) fixed partition; positive = community hub, negative = bridge. Closed-form vectorised update (one matrix product nodes); matches brute-force igraph::modularity() deletion random directed, undirected weighted graphs. Requires membership; wrong-length input raises cograph_bad_membership. centrality_neighborhood_connectivity() (tau 0.64) — Maslov & Sneppen (2002). title: cograph 2.1.0
text: measures don’t fit per-node centrality() data frame, live standalone functions: estrada_index() — graph-level spectral invariant: , equal trace matrix exponential adjacency. Equivalently, sum subgraph_centrality() across nodes. Matches networkx.estrada_index machine epsilon (max relative diff ~5e-15 across random test graphs). trophic_incoherence() — graph-level food-web stability measure (Johnson et al. 2014). Defined population standard deviation per-edge trophic differences   trophic level node . Zero perfectly coherent DAGs (e.g., pure chain). Matches networkx.trophic_incoherence_parameter machine epsilon. Directed-; reuses existing trophic_level calculator. group_centrality(x, nodes, measure = c("betweenness", "closeness", "degree")) — Everett-Borgatti (1999) group centrality set nodes. Returns scalar. Supports mode = ""/"" directed-degree variants. Group closeness group degree match networkx.group_*_centrality bit-exact. Group betweenness implements textbook Everett-Borgatti / Puzis 2008 definition (fraction shortest paths passing least one node group), diverges networkx.group_betweenness_centrality graphs due known quirk NetworkX’s Puzis-Yahalom-Elovici iterative algorithm. Verified via independent Python brute-force: cograph matches textbook definition; NX produces larger values graphs many overlapping shortest paths. Documented roxygen “Divergence NetworkX” section. dispersion(x, u = NULL, v = NULL, normalized = TRUE, alpha = 1, b = 0, c = 0) — Backstrom-Kleinberg (2014 Facebook) pair-level measure tie strength. Counts number “well-dispersed” mutual friends u v (pairs common neighbors directly connected share common neighbor inside u’s ego network u v). Matches networkx.dispersion bit-exact across 156 edges karate club graph. Returns scalar, named vector, data frame depending u, v specified.

Implemented natively (runtime dependency sna). R-level source). Directed-; warns returns NA undirected input.

Directed-; returns NA warning undirected input. centrality_prestige_domain_proximity() — distance-weighted variant: R_v^2 / (D_v * (n - 1)) R_v number reachers D_v sum geodesic distances v. what: Centrality Batch 3 — classical measures with reference-package validation
title: cograph 2.1.0
text: centrality_katz() — Katz (1953) status index. Bit-exact match centiserve::katzcent (cograph mirrors centiserve’s exact LAPACK call sequence). Also matches igraph::alpha_centrality(exo = 1) networkx.katz_centrality_numpy machine epsilon. New katz_alpha parameter (default 0.1). centrality_hubbell() — Hubbell (1965) input-output centrality. Bit-exact match centiserve::hubbell (cograph mirrors centiserve’s full-inverse LAPACK call path). Note: centiserve’s default (weights = NULL) silently ignores E(g)$weight; reproduce cograph’s behavior centiserve weighted graphs, pass weights = igraph::E(g)$weight explicitly. New hubbell_weight parameter (default 0.5). centrality_information() — Stephenson-Zelen (1989) information centrality. Bit-exact match sna::infocent connected undirected graphs (cograph mirrors sna’s exact construction solve() call sequence). centrality_pairwisedis() — Pairwise disconnectivity (Potapov et al. 2008). Directed-; fraction reachable ordered pairs become unreachable node removed. Bit-exact match centiserve::pairwisedis. Warns returns NA undirected input, matching convention used salsa, leaderrank, trophic_level. centrality_reaching_local() / reaching_global() — Local global reaching centrality (Mones, Vicsek & Vicsek 2012). Bit-exact match networkx.local_reaching_centrality across directed unweighted, undirected unweighted, weighted branches. Undirected unweighted LRC coincides igraph::harmonic_centrality(normalized = TRUE) (documented). reaching_global() graph-level hierarchy statistic [0, 1].
